newsitem.title: SINGAPORE: U.S warns labour issue jeopardises world trade deal.
newsitem.headline: U.S warns labour issue jeopardises world trade deal.

text.p: The United States warned on Tuesday it might block a declaration by the World Trade Organisation to point the way toward free global trade unless the text raised the issue of cheap labour, negotiators said.
The deadlock on the second day of the WTO's ministerial conference came in late-night closed-door talks on whether the final document should refer to ending labour rights abuses.

Several diplomats emerging from the negotiations said Washington had taken a tough stand on its demand, which many developing nations fear is being used as a means of eroding the developing world's commercial advantage of cheap labour.

The United States had indicated in the talks that unless it won mention of the labour issue in the final declaration it would not accept several other parts of the document -- repeating a threat it had already made in Geneva that it would block a declaration unless it got its way, envoys said.
But WTO Director-General Renato Ruggiero told Reuters that he was pleased with the level of progress on an issue that has emerged as the most divisive at the Singapore meeting.
"We are making good progress, I am very encouraged," he said.
"It's going a lot better than I expected," he said, adding that one Asian country that had been taking a very strong line had "made a very useful proposal". Envoys identified the country as Malaysia.

Diplomats emerging from the meeting said the discussions would resume on Wednesday and possibly stretch into Thursday to try to hammer out an agreement acceptable to all sides, with Ruggiero chairing talks among various nations.
"But there are some very hard positions still being taken," said one envoy.

Pakistani ambassador to the WTO, Munir Akram, said his country -- which had been a tough opponent of any mention of labour -- had proposed the issue be mentioned in a chairman's statement at the end of the conference rather than in the declaration.
He said this proposal had been backed by many countries, inclding several developing countries.
But he declined to say exactly what the U.S. reaction had been. Other diplomats said it had been flatly rejected by the United States and the European Union, reflecting the strong stand of France.
Washington had made absolutely clear it would not accept a side statement as a vehicle to cover the labour issue, they said.
"This has been the most difficult issue and that was evident tonight," WTO spokesman Keith Rockwell told reporters.
"There was some progress on this issue this evening, but it has been and continues to be a thorny issue and difficult to resolve," he said.
All the signs are that Washington is fighting a losing battle.
Opponents argue, with support from several European nations and Australia, that the method of making goods is no business of an organisation dedicated to regulating international trade.
They believe that behind fine western words on improving the lot of the poor is a bid to use the WTO to impose penalties on goods produced by cheap labour in the developing world.
